title: Authorize, don’t authenticate
excerpt: Hold on to your data by keeping it in your own database
content_html:
The login screen of any web application is the equivalent of that application telling you “In order to access YOUR data in MY database, prove you are who you say you are.” You’re authenticating with the application so that you can have the privilege of giving it your data.

In a previous blog post, I covered the downside to applications controlling your data. An application’s owner can restrict your access to your own data. They can delete the data. They can sell the data to a third party. They might introduce a bug that allows other people to access the data. They might get compromised. Or they can avoid all of this just to modify their policies down the road or see changes in ownership or management.

In a word: poppycock. It’s your data! You shouldn’t have to prove to anyone else that you have the right to access it. No one should tell you how to use your own data. And no one should do anything with your data that you aren’t comfortable with.

To gain agency over your data, you have to have agency over the database in which it lives1. If you own the database, you actually own the data. But running a database is a serious undertaking that we can’t expect from the average internet user. And even if you run a personal database, how should applications interact with it?

Over the past few months, I’ve explored the concept of personal database authorization, which allows you to give an application access to a database you control. Specifically, I built an authorization flow into ayb, my project to make it easy to create databases, share them with collaborators, and query them from anywhere. Here’s a video of how you can grant an application access to a freshly created database you own. Critically, the application has no login screen, instead asking for a database where your data will live:
Authorization in action: A to-do application with no login screen that requests access to a database you control. Todos is the to-do list application I created and use as my daily driver.

Holding on to your data

Here are three principles behind what’s happening in the video:

Authorize, don’t authenticate. In traditional web applications, you authenticate with the application to log in/prove your identity. Only once you’ve proved yourself with a password/passkey/… can you get access to your data. That puts the application in charge of your data. Instead, you should authorize an application to get access to your personal database. In the video, you see Todos asking you to Connect your database (“authorize me!”) rather than Enter your password (“authenticate yourself!”). The technology to support this flow is well understood and widely used: Todos initiates an OAuth2 flow to ask ayb for a token with which to query a database. I’ve open sourced an ayb.js library that manages these OAuth2 interactions on behalf of an application, and an engineer can integrate it into a new application in under an hour.

Creating a database should be as easy as creating a document. Most users can open up Microsoft Word or Google Drive and create an empty document. On the other hand, most users don’t know how to set up a Postgres database that backs itself up periodically and can be connected to a running application. In the video, the authorization flow allows you to pick an existing database or create a new one, and creating a new database is as easy as picking a name for it. If you create a database, you’ll receive periodic snapshots/backups without any configuration, and the application knows how to speak with ayb, run migrations, and store data in it. The database creation flow is no more difficult than one to create a file on your computer or the cloud, which is a lot more than you can say for most databases today.

Applications should store as little as possible outside a user’s database. The Todos application in the video is static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It knows nothing about its visitors. I assume somewhere in my server logs I can find the IP address of anyone that downloads the static resource, but beyond that, the application stores no state on my servers. For added privacy, you can download a self-contained index.html file and self-host the application. When you first load Todos, it asks you to Connect to your database to get started. Once it has a token with which to query your database2, all of your intimate to-do list items are stored in that database you own. You can revoke Todos’ access any time.

Trusting your host

Having just celebrated the virtues of storing data in a database you control, I have to deflate the balloon a bit. So far, I effectively said “don’t store your data with someone else, store it in something called ayb.” ayb is open source and while you CAN host it for yourself, do you want to? I believe ayb is pretty easy to install and run, but I certainly don’t think every user should become a database administrator. This leaves users with a frustrating choice: trade their trust of third-party applications for their trust of third-party database hosts. Are we just trading one form of centralization for another?

I think there’s still benefit to separating applications from the databases that they operate on. For starters, you actually get choice: rather than implicitly having to accept that every app developer is a custodian of a slice of your data, you get to pick where your data lives one time, regardless of how many applications you use. The abstraction means that once you get the hang of a tool like ayb, you can use it for multiple applications, which hopefully amortizes the cost of regaining agency over your data. You can pick who hosts your data because ayb is open source. I dream of a day when cooperatives and organizations that want to offer users agency over their data can offer alternatives to self-hosting and compete to be the custodian of your data. Finally, ayb doesn’t invent file formats: your data is stored in boring, well-accepted file formats like SQLite’s and DuckDB’s3. I’m planning to add export and import endpoints soon to make it easier to walk away with your data and bring it to another host.

Beyond personal data: collaboration and social interactions

The “authorize, don’t authenticate” model works most smoothly for situations where you definitively “own” the data. The more the dataset is the result of collaboration or social interaction, the less clear it is who owns the data, and the harder it is to authorize access.

Collaboration is one place where the definition of “personal data” is fuzzier. If you are working on a document on your own, it’s easy to tell an application to store “my document” in “my database.” But if you’re using something like a collaborative editor, say Google Documents, and are working on a document with someone else, what does it mean to store that document in a “personal database?” ayb lets you share your database with collaborators, but each database still has an owner. It would be interesting to explore models of collaborative personal databases, where users authorize an application to keep both of their databases in sync for data that they are collaborating on, but it’s beyond anything I’ve built, prototyped, or have my head wrapped around.

Social data is another type of data based on collaboration. We’ve seen the downsides of large organizations storing our social media data and also owning the algorithms and interfaces that control how that data is displayed to us. Projects such as ActivityPub/Mastodon and AT Protocol/Bluesky offer users more choice as to where their social data is stored, in different ways (ActivityPub’s federation vs. AT Protocol’s separation of storage and aggregation). Still, there’s a catch: these projects offer options on where to store your data, but the stored data is not useful until it’s aggregated into a timeline with everyone else’s. Solutions for timeline aggregation tend to fall back to centralization, as few people want to stomach the infrastructure and operational concerns involved in keeping track of what millions of people are saying in aggregate. Given how easy it is to create a static HTML/CSS/JavaScript application that can access and update your personal database, I’d love to see a decentralized extreme that displays your social network’s recent updates aggregated across all their personal data stores without relying on a centralized aggregator.

Where we go from here

Ultimately, I hope more people build software that asks users to authorize access to personal databases rather than asking users to authenticate with a centralized database. I’ve started doing this for my own personal applications, from tracking my Todos to tracking my Streaks to even managing newsletter subscriptions on my blog. Since ayb lets me spin up a database with the click of a button, I’ve built applications I previously avoided creating because I didn’t want to store my sensitive data in someone else’s database, but also didn’t have the time to administer my own.

To build on all of this, here are a few areas I’m excited to explore from here:

  • Supporting basic collaboration, such as how multiple users like journalists or scientists might collaborate on a dataset they are curating.
  • Investigating how this all connects to the local-first community. You’re in control of your ayb database, but it’s still hosted remotely, and I’m curious how a local SQLite/DuckDB database might sync with the remote one.
  • Identifying ways to help other application developers build software in a way that leaves users with agency over their data.

But mostly, I want to see how many login screens we can replace with database authorization screens. If you want to collaborate on any of these topics, or want help building software around personal databases, reach out!

Thank you to Meredith Blumenstock for giving feedback on the blog post and video.

  1. I’m certainly not the first to argue for data agency. Sir Tim Berners-Lee’s Solid Project has been exploring the idea of personal data pods for years. The ActivityPub and AT Protocol communities are building social networks that put users in more control of their shared content. The local-first community argues that users should have more control over their own data. My aim is to show how we can string together familiar, off-the-shelf technologies to make it easier for developers to build applications that offer more control. ↩

  2. To accomplish this, ayb.js implements OAuth2 using PKCE, which allows an ayb token to be issued to any app, even if it’s a fully static frontend blob with no backend to serve a client secret. ↩

  3. I’m iterating on an open PR for DuckDB, so coming soon. ↩

sentences.en: In the video, the authorization flow allows you to pick an existing database or create a new one, and creating a new database is as easy as picking a name for it.

blocks.html_en: Applications should store as little as possible outside a user’s database. The Todos application in the video is static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It knows nothing about its visitors. I assume somewhere in my server logs I can find the IP address of anyone that downloads the static resource, but beyond that, the application stores no state on my servers. For added privacy, you can download a self-contained index.html file and self-host the application. When you first load Todos, it asks you to Connect to your database to get started. Once it has a token with which to query your database2, all of your intimate to-do list items are stored in that database you own. You can revoke Todos’ access any time.

blocks.html_en: Trusting your host

sentences.en: Trusting your host
sentences.zh: 信任你的主人

blocks.html_en: Having just celebrated the virtues of storing data in a database you control, I have to deflate the balloon a bit. So far, I effectively said “don’t store your data with someone else, store it in something called ayb.” ayb is open source and while you CAN host it for yourself, do you want to? I believe ayb is pretty easy to install and run, but I certainly don’t think every user should become a database administrator. This leaves users with a frustrating choice: trade their trust of third-party applications for their trust of third-party database hosts. Are we just trading one form of centralization for another?

sentences.en: Having just celebrated the virtues of storing data in a database you control, I have to deflate the balloon a bit.
sentences.zh: 刚刚庆祝了将数据存储在您控制的数据库中的优点之后，我必须把气球放气一点。

sentences.en: So far, I effectively said “don’t store your data with someone else, store it in something called ayb.”
sentences.zh: 到目前为止，我实际上是在说“不要将您的数据存储在其他人处，而是将其存储在名为 ayb 的东西中。”

sentences.en: ayb is open source and while you CAN host it for yourself, do you want to?
sentences.zh: ayb 是开源的，虽然您可以自己托管它，但您愿意吗？

sentences.en: I believe ayb is pretty easy to install and run, but I certainly don’t think every user should become a database administrator.
sentences.zh: 我相信 ayb 非常容易安装和运行，但我当然不认为每个用户都应该成为数据库管理员。

sentences.en: This leaves users with a frustrating choice: trade their trust of third-party applications for their trust of third-party database hosts.
sentences.zh: 这给用户带来了一个令人沮丧的选择：用对第三方应用程序的信任来换取对第三方数据库主机的信任。

sentences.en: Are we just trading one form of centralization for another?
sentences.zh: 我们是否只是用一种形式的集中化来换取另一种形式的集中化？

blocks.html_en: I think there’s still benefit to separating applications from the databases that they operate on. For starters, you actually get choice: rather than implicitly having to accept that every app developer is a custodian of a slice of your data, you get to pick where your data lives one time, regardless of how many applications you use. The abstraction means that once you get the hang of a tool like ayb, you can use it for multiple applications, which hopefully amortizes the cost of regaining agency over your data. You can pick who hosts your data because ayb is open source. I dream of a day when cooperatives and organizations that want to offer users agency over their data can offer alternatives to self-hosting and compete to be the custodian of your data. Finally, ayb doesn’t invent file formats: your data is stored in boring, well-accepted file formats like SQLite’s and DuckDB’s3. I’m planning to add export and import endpoints soon to make it easier to walk away with your data and bring it to another host.

blocks.html_en: Beyond personal data: collaboration and social interactions

sentences.en: Beyond personal data: collaboration and social interactions
sentences.zh: 超越个人数据：协作和社交互动

blocks.html_en: The “authorize, don’t authenticate” model works most smoothly for situations where you definitively “own” the data. The more the dataset is the result of collaboration or social interaction, the less clear it is who owns the data, and the harder it is to authorize access.

sentences.en: The “authorize, don’t authenticate” model works most smoothly for situations where you definitively “own” the data.
sentences.zh: 在您明确“拥有”数据的情况下，“授权，不验证”模型运行得最顺利。

sentences.en: The more the dataset is the result of collaboration or social interaction, the less clear it is who owns the data, and the harder it is to authorize access.
sentences.zh: 数据集越是协作或社交互动的结果，谁拥有这些数据就越不明确，授权访问也就越困难。

blocks.html_en: Collaboration is one place where the definition of “personal data” is fuzzier. If you are working on a document on your own, it’s easy to tell an application to store “my document” in “my database.” But if you’re using something like a collaborative editor, say Google Documents, and are working on a document with someone else, what does it mean to store that document in a “personal database?” ayb lets you share your database with collaborators, but each database still has an owner. It would be interesting to explore models of collaborative personal databases, where users authorize an application to keep both of their databases in sync for data that they are collaborating on, but it’s beyond anything I’ve built, prototyped, or have my head wrapped around.

sentences.en: Collaboration is one place where the definition of “personal data” is fuzzier.
sentences.zh: 协作是“个人数据”定义较为模糊的一个领域。

sentences.en: If you are working on a document on your own, it’s easy to tell an application to store “my document” in “my database.”

blocks.html_en: Social data is another type of data based on collaboration. We’ve seen the downsides of large organizations storing our social media data and also owning the algorithms and interfaces that control how that data is displayed to us. Projects such as ActivityPub/Mastodon and AT Protocol/Bluesky offer users more choice as to where their social data is stored, in different ways (ActivityPub’s federation vs. AT Protocol’s separation of storage and aggregation). Still, there’s a catch: these projects offer options on where to store your data, but the stored data is not useful until it’s aggregated into a timeline with everyone else’s. Solutions for timeline aggregation tend to fall back to centralization, as few people want to stomach the infrastructure and operational concerns involved in keeping track of what millions of people are saying in aggregate. Given how easy it is to create a static HTML/CSS/JavaScript application that can access and update your personal database, I’d love to see a decentralized extreme that displays your social network’s recent updates aggregated across all their personal data stores without relying on a centralized aggregator.

blocks.html_en: Where we go from here

sentences.en: Where we go from here
sentences.zh: 我们从这里去哪里

blocks.html_en: Ultimately, I hope more people build software that asks users to authorize access to personal databases rather than asking users to authenticate with a centralized database. I’ve started doing this for my own personal applications, from tracking my Todos to tracking my Streaks to even managing newsletter subscriptions on my blog. Since ayb lets me spin up a database with the click of a button, I’ve built applications I previously avoided creating because I didn’t want to store my sensitive data in someone else’s database, but also didn’t have the time to administer my own.

blocks.html_en: • I’m certainly not the first to argue for data agency. Sir Tim Berners-Lee’s Solid Project has been exploring the idea of personal data pods for years. The ActivityPub and AT Protocol communities are building social networks that put users in more control of their shared content. The local-first community argues that users should have more control over their own data. My aim is to show how we can string together familiar, off-the-shelf technologies to make it easier for developers to build applications that offer more control. ↩

content_html_zh:
任何 Web 应用程序的登录屏幕都相当于该应用程序告诉您“为了访问我的数据库中的数据，请证明您的身份。” 您正在使用该应用程序进行身份验证，以便您有权向其提供您的数据。

在之前的博客文章中，我介绍了控制数据的应用程序的缺点。 应用程序的所有者可以限制您对自己数据的访问。 他们可以删除数据。 他们可以将数据出售给第三方。 他们可能会引入一个允许其他人访问数据的错误。 他们可能会受到损害。 或者，他们可以避免所有这些，只是为了以后修改政策或看到所有权或管理权的变化。

简而言之：胡说八道。 这是你的数据！ 您不必向其他人证明您有权访问它。 没有人应该告诉您如何使用自己的数据。 任何人都不应该对您的数据做任何您不喜欢的事情。

为了获得对数据的代理权，您必须对数据所在的数据库拥有代理权1。 如果您拥有数据库，那么您实际上就拥有数据。 但运行数据库是一项严肃的任务，我们不能指望普通互联网用户能做到这一点。 即使您运行个人数据库，应用程序应该如何与其交互？

在过去的几个月里，我探索了个人数据库授权的概念，它允许您向应用程序授予对您控制的数据库的访问权限。 具体来说，我在我的项目 ayb 中构建了一个授权流程，以便轻松创建数据库、与协作者共享数据库以及从任何地方查询数据库。 以下视频介绍了如何授予应用程序访问您拥有的新创建的数据库的权限。 重要的是，该应用程序没有登录屏幕，而是要求提供数据所在的数据库：
实际授权：没有登录屏幕的待办事项应用程序，请求访问您控制的数据库。 Todos 是我创建的待办事项列表应用程序，并将其用作我的日常驱动程序。

保留您的数据

以下是视频中发生的事情背后的三个原则：

授权，不验证。 在传统的 Web 应用程序中，您通过应用程序进行身份验证以登录/证明您的身份。 只有当您使用密码/密钥/...证明自己时 您可以访问您的数据吗？ 这使得应用程序负责您的数据。 相反，您应该授权应用程序访问您的个人数据库。 在视频中，您看到 Todos 要求您连接数据库（“授权我！”）而不是输入密码（“验证您自己的身份！”）。 支持此流程的技术已被广泛理解并广泛使用：Todos 启动 OAuth2 流程，向 ayb 请求用于查询数据库的令牌。 我开源了一个 ayb.js 库，它代表应用程序管理这些 OAuth2 交互，工程师可以在一小时内将其集成到新应用程序中。

创建数据库应该像创建文档一样简单。 大多数用户可以打开 Microsoft Word 或 Google Drive 并创建一个空文档。 另一方面，大多数用户不知道如何设置一个定期备份并可以连接到正在运行的应用程序的 Postgres 数据库。 在视频中，授权流程允许您选择现有数据库或创建新数据库，创建新数据库就像为其选择名称一样简单。 如果您创建数据库，您将收到定期快照/备份，无需任何配置，并且应用程序知道如何与 ayb 通信、运行迁移以及在其中存储数据。 数据库创建流程并不比在计算机或云上创建文件更困难，这比您对当今大多数数据库所说的要困难得多。

应用程序应尽可能少地在用户数据库之外存储数据。 视频中的 Todos 应用程序是静态 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript。 它对访客一无所知。 我假设在我的服务器日志中的某个位置我可以找到下载静态资源的任何人的 IP 地址，但除此之外，应用程序在我的服务器上不存储任何状态。 为了增加隐私，您可以下载独立的index.html 文件并自行托管该应用程序。 当您第一次加载 Todos 时，它会要求您连接到数据库才能开始。 一旦它拥有用于查询数据库的令牌2，您所有的私密待办事项列表项都会存储在您拥有的数据库中。 您可以随时撤销 Todos 的访问权限。

信任你的主人

刚刚庆祝了将数据存储在您控制的数据库中的优点之后，我必须把气球放气一点。 到目前为止，我实际上是在说“不要将您的数据存储在其他人处，而是将其存储在名为 ayb 的东西中。” ayb 是开源的，虽然您可以自己托管它，但您愿意吗？ 我相信 ayb 非常容易安装和运行，但我当然不认为每个用户都应该成为数据库管理员。 这给用户带来了一个令人沮丧的选择：用对第三方应用程序的信任来换取对第三方数据库主机的信任。 我们是否只是用一种形式的集中化来换取另一种形式的集中化？

我认为将应用程序与其运行的数据库分开仍然有好处。 对于初学者来说，您实际上可以选择：无论您使用多少个应用程序，您都可以一次选择数据所在的位置，而不是隐式地接受每个应用程序开发人员都是一部分数据的保管人。 这种抽象意味着一旦您掌握了像 ayb 这样的工具，您就可以将其用于多个应用程序，这有望分摊重新获得数据代理权的成本。 您可以选择谁托管您的数据，因为 ayb 是开源的。 我梦想有一天，想要为用户提供数据代理权的合作社和组织可以提供自托管的替代方案，并竞争成为数据的托管人。 最后，ayb 并没有发明文件格式：您的数据以无聊的、广为接受的文件格式存储，例如 SQLite 和 DuckDB3。 我计划很快添加导出和导入端点，以便更轻松地带走您的数据并将其带到另一台主机。

超越个人数据：协作和社交互动

在您明确“拥有”数据的情况下，“授权，不验证”模型运行得最顺利。 数据集越是协作或社交互动的结果，谁拥有这些数据就越不明确，授权访问也就越困难。

协作是“个人数据”定义较为模糊的一个领域。 如果您自己处理文档，则很容易告诉应用程序将“我的文档”存储在“我的数据库”中。 但是，如果您正在使用协作编辑器（例如 Google Documents）之类的工具，并且正在与其他人一起处理文档，那么将该文档存储在“个人数据库”中意味着什么？ ayb 允许您与协作者共享数据库，但每个数据库仍然有一个所有者。 探索协作个人数据库的模型会很有趣，在该模型中，用户授权应用程序使两个数据库保持同步，以获取他们正在协作的数据，但这超出了我构建、原型化或思考的任何内容。

社交数据是另一种基于协作的数据。 我们已经看到大型组织存储我们的社交媒体数据并拥有控制这些数据如何向我们显示的算法和界面的缺点。 ActivityPub/Mastodon 和 AT Protocol/Bluesky 等项目以不同的方式为用户提供了更多关于社交数据存储位置的选择（ActivityPub 的联合与 AT Protocol 的存储和聚合分离）。 不过，有一个问题：这些项目提供了数据存储位置的选项，但存储的数据只有在与其他人的数据聚合到时间线中后才有用。 时间线聚合的解决方案往往会回归集中化，因为很少有人愿意忍受跟踪数百万人的总体言论所涉及的基础设施和运营问题。 鉴于创建一个可以访问和更新个人数据库的静态 HTML/CSS/JavaScript 应用程序是多么容易，我希望看到一个去中心化的极端，它可以显示您的社交网络在所有个人数据存储中聚合的最近更新，而不依赖于集中式聚合器。

我们从这里去哪里

最终，我希望更多的人构建要求用户授权访问个人数据库的软件，而不是要求用户使用集中式数据库进行身份验证。 我已经开始为自己的个人应用程序执行此操作，从跟踪我的待办事项到跟踪我的条纹，甚至管理博客上的时事通讯订阅。 由于 ayb 让我只需单击一个按钮即可启动数据库，因此我构建了以前避免创建的应用程序，因为我不想将敏感数据存储在别人的数据库中，但也没有时间管理自己的数据库。

在此基础上，我很高兴从这里探索以下几个领域：

  • 支持基本协作，例如记者或科学家等多个用户如何在他们正在管理的数据集上进行协作。
  • 调查这一切如何与本地优先社区联系起来。 您可以控制 ayb 数据库，但它仍然是远程托管的，我很好奇本地 SQLite/DuckDB 数据库如何与远程数据库同步。
  • 确定帮助其他应用程序开发人员构建软件的方法，让用户对其数据拥有代理权。

但最重要的是，我想看看我们可以用数据库授权屏幕替换多少登录屏幕。 如果您想就这些主题进行协作，或者需要帮助围绕个人数据库构建软件，请联系我们！
